The City-Country Gap:

text: Urban Breakthrough and Green Uprising One crucial political result of modernization is the gap it pro- duces between countryside and city.
text_raw:
Urban Breakthrough and
Green Uprising
One crucial political result of modernization is the gap it pro-
duces between countryside and city.

text: This gap is, indeed, a preemi- nent political characteristic of societies undergoing rapid social and economic change.
text_raw:
This gap is, indeed, a preemi-
nent political characteristic of societies undergoing rapid social
and economic change.

text: It is the primary source of political instabil- ity in such societies and a principal, if not the principal, obstacle to national integration.
text_raw:
It is the primary source of political instabil-
ity in such societies and a principal, if not the principal, obstacle
to national integration.

text: Modernization is, in large part, measured by the growth of the city.
text_raw:
Modernization is, in large part, measured
by the growth of the city.

text: The city becomes the locus of new eco- nomic activities, new social classes, new culture and education, which make it fundamentally different from the more tradition- bound countryside.
text_raw:
The city becomes the locus of new eco-
nomic activities, new social classes, new culture and education,
which make it fundamentally different from the more tradition-
bound countryside.

text: At the same time modernization may also im- pose new demands on the countryside which intensify its hostility toward the city.

At the same time modernization may also im-
pose new demands on the countryside which intensify its hostility
toward the city.

text: The city dweller's feelings of intellectual superior- ity to and contempt for the backward peasant are matched by the country dweller's feelings of moral superiority to and yet envy of the city slicker.
text_raw:
The city dweller's feelings of intellectual superior-
ity to and contempt for the backward peasant are matched by the
country dweller's feelings of moral superiority to and yet envy of
the city slicker.

text: The city and the countryside become different na- tions, different ways of life.
text_raw:

tions, different ways of life.

text_raw:
Historically, the emigration of the peasant from village cottage
to city slum was a decisive and irreversible change.

text: In the later modernizing countries, however, the very process of moderniza- tion itself has made the move less decisive and has reduced the gap between city and countryside.
text_raw:

modernizing countries, however, the very process of moderniza-
tion itself has made the move less decisive and has reduced the gap
between city and countryside.

text: "The English constitution, in a word," Bagehot argued, "is framed on the prin- ciple of choosing a single sovereign authority, and making it good: the American, upon the principle of having many sovereign au- thorities, and hoping that their multitude may atone for their in- feriority." 40 Fifty years later Pollard could similarly point to the separation of powers as "the reason why American efficiency, so marked in private concerns, has been so fettered in government" and why "American politics are unattractive to so many American minds." be able, first, to innovate policy, that is, to promote social and eco-

In the bureaucratic state, on the other hand, "the central power conscripts a consid- erable portion of the social wealth by taxation and uses it first to maintain a military establishment and then to support a more or less extensive number of public services." text: The mwami or king of Ruanda "was an absolute monarch who governed through a highly centralized organization and by principles that enabled him effectively to control his militarily powerful feudatories." In Urundi, on the other hand, the king shared power with the royal clan or baganwa, whose members "were by hereditary right the ruling class of Urundi." In Ruanda the king might make grants of land to members of the royal family, but they "had no special rights or powers." The baganwa of Urundi, however, could ap- point their own subordinates "to lead their personal armies and to administer their lands." Not infrequently these personal armies, in typical feudal fashion, would be used against the king.
